blocks.content: Some shared resources are read constantly but written to rarely. Treating every access the same way, with one simple lock, wastes a huge amount of potential concurrency. The Readers Writers Problem is about doing better.
1. The Setup
A shared resource, like a database record or a file, is accessed by multiple READER threads and multiple WRITER threads. Readers only look at the data, they never change it. Writers modify it.

Because readers do not change anything, multiple readers can safely access the resource at the exact same time with no risk of corruption. A writer is different: it needs completely exclusive access, no readers and no other writers allowed while it is working.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408559626-79510799.png
2. Why a Plain Lock Is Not Good Enough
blocks.text: 2. Why a Plain Lock Is Not Good Enough

blocks.content: The simplest possible solution is a single ordinary lock: whoever wants access, reader or writer, must acquire it first. This is correct, nothing ever gets corrupted, but it is needlessly slow.

It forces every reader to wait in line one at a time, even though none of them would actually conflict with each other. On a resource that is read far more often than it is written, this serialization throws away most of the available concurrency for no real safety benefit.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408559626-251353160.png
blocks.alt: Why a Plain Lock Is Not Good Enough

blocks.content: 3. Solution One: Readers Preference

The first classic solution tracks a read count. The FIRST reader to arrive locks out writers on behalf of the whole group. Every reader after that just increments the count and proceeds immediately, no locking needed since a writer is already excluded.
When a reader finishes, it decrements the count. The LAST reader to leave, the one that brings the count back to zero, is the one that unlocks the resource for writers.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408559627-300560128.png
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408559627-952938795.png
4. The Starvation Risk of Readers Preference
blocks.text: 4. The Starvation Risk of Readers Preference

blocks.content: This solution has a serious flaw. If readers keep arriving continuously, there is effectively never a moment when the reader count reaches zero, so a waiting writer can be starved indefinitely.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408559627-330723157.png
blocks.alt: The Starvation Risk of Readers Preference

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.content: A resource that is read constantly and rarely written to is exactly the situation where readers preference performs worst for writers.
5. Solution Two: Writers Preference
The second classic solution flips the priority. Once a writer is waiting, any NEW readers are blocked from starting, even though they would not technically conflict with the currently active readers.
This guarantees a waiting writer will get in once the current readers finish, solving writer starvation. But now the reverse problem exists, a steady stream of writers can starve readers instead.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408559627-7480818.png
6. A Fair Solution

A third approach uses a queue and serves both readers and writers roughly in arrival order, so neither side can starve the other indefinitely. This is more complex to implement but is what production grade libraries generally aim for.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408559627-544931873.png
7. Real World Usage: ReadWriteLock

An in memory cache read by many threads but updated only occasionally is a textbook instance of this exact pattern. Many languages provide a dedicated ReadWriteLock or RWLock primitive built specifically for this problem, so you rarely need to implement the semaphore logic by hand.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408559628-271634676.png

8. Common Mistakes

["Using a plain mutex for the whole resource and needlessly serializing every read, throwing away the concurrency the problem is meant to unlock.","Picking readers preference by default without realizing it can starve writers indefinitely under sustained read load."]

Picking readers preference by default without realizing it can starve writers indefinitely under sustained read load.

blocks.content: 9. Interview Angle

Being able to name both preference variants, readers preference and writers preference, and explain precisely which side each one can starve, is exactly what separates a memorized definition from real understanding of this problem.
